prompt: What does a configuration scanner such as Checkov read when it scans `~/shop`?
hint: It needs no credentials.

choices.text: The resources in the AWS account, through the API
choices.why: That would need credentials and an API; a configuration scan uses neither.

choices.text: The state file, to know what was applied
choices.why: The scanner never opens the state; it reads the text of the configuration.

choices.text: The `.tf` files
choices.why: Yes. It parses the configuration and holds each resource against its rules.

choices.text: The output of the last `terraform plan`, saved by Terraform
choices.why: A plan can be scanned, but only when you save it and pass it explicitly; `-d .` reads files.

prompt: A colleague opened port 22 to `0.0.0.0/0` by hand with the aws CLI. Checkov then reports `PASSED` for `CKV_AWS_24` on every resource. Why?
hint: Where does that rule exist?

choices.text: Because none of the files mention port 22, and the rule exists only in the account
choices.why: Right. The scan is correct about the text, and the account is outside what it reads; a plan finds this.

choices.text: Moto does not report hand-made rules
choices.why: `describe-security-groups` showed the rule; Checkov simply never asked AWS.

choices.text: `CKV_AWS_24` checks only port 443
choices.why: Its title is about port 22, and it failed on `ssh.tf` once the rule was in a file.

choices.text: It needs `--skip-download` removed to see live rules
choices.why: The download is guidelines and severities, not the account's resources.

prompt: Which of these are outside what a scan of the configuration can see? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about where each fact lives.

choices.text: A value passed at plan time with `-var-file`
choices.why: Yes; nothing in the directory says what it will be.

choices.text: A rule typed into the account by hand
choices.why: Yes; it exists only in AWS.

choices.text: A bucket with no public access block resource
choices.why: That is a fact about the files, and `CKV2_AWS_6` found it.

choices.text: `0.0.0.0/0` written literally in `ssh.tf`
choices.why: It is in the text; Checkov and Trivy both reported it.

choices.text: Whether anybody still needs the SSH rule
choices.why: Yes; that is a judgement about the system, not the text.

prompt: Ana runs Checkov offline with `--skip-download`. What does she lose compared with a connected run?
hint: What was the download for?

choices.text: Every check written for AWS
choices.why: The checks are in the package; 35 ran offline.

choices.text: Severities and guide links
choices.why: Right. Both come from Prisma Cloud's guidelines, and the checks carry no severity of their own.

choices.text: The ability to scan anything but Terraform files
choices.why: The frameworks are local too; the download is only metadata.

choices.text: File names and line numbers in findings
choices.why: Every offline finding still printed `File: /ssh.tf:1-8` and the like.

prompt: The Checkov flag that stops it asking Prisma Cloud's API for guidelines on every run is `--___`.
hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.

prompt: `CKV2_AWS_6` says the bucket has no public access block, although the bucket resource itself has no argument for one. How can the check know?
hint: Look at the prefix of the id.

choices.text: It asks S3 for the bucket's settings
choices.why: Checkov never calls AWS.

choices.text: It searches the configuration for another resource pointing at the bucket
choices.why: Yes. `CKV2_` checks look at connections between resources, here an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block`.

choices.text: It assumes every bucket is public
choices.why: It does not assume; it found no block pointing at this bucket.

choices.text: It reads the state file
choices.why: A configuration scan does not open the state.

prompt: Ana's custom check `CKV2_SHOP_1` passed `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.https`, which allows `0.0.0.0/0`. Why?
hint: The definition has two branches joined by `or`.

choices.text: Port 443 is not port 22, so the first branch holds
choices.why: Right. The rule only restricts rules for port 22.

choices.text: Custom checks never fail a resource that a built-in check already passed
choices.why: Checks are independent; it failed the SSH rule regardless of other results.

choices.text: HTTPS is exempt in every Checkov rule
choices.why: Nothing exempts HTTPS; the YAML decides.
It is the other way round, and the check compares with `equals`, not containment.

prompt: Two pipelines run the same Trivy binary on the same commit, one with network and one without. Their reports differ. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Where can Trivy's checks come from?

choices.text: Trivy picks a random sample of checks on each run, and a run with network samples more of them
choices.why: Nothing is random; the difference is which set of checks was loaded.

choices.text: The connected one downloaded a newer checks bundle
choices.why: Yes. The other fell back to the checks embedded in the binary.

choices.text: Without network Trivy scans only `main.tf` and skips the other files in the directory
choices.why: Offline it reported both `main.tf` and `ssh.tf`.

choices.text: Severities need the network
choices.why: That is Checkov. Trivy's severities ship with each check.

prompt: Trivy reported `AWS-0107` for the SSH rule and nothing for the HTTPS rule, which also allows `0.0.0.0/0`. Why?
hint: Read the check's own explanation.

choices.text: The check is about remote administration ports such as 22 and 3389
choices.why: Yes; port 443 open to the world is the point of a web server.

choices.text: The HTTPS rule has a description
choices.why: Both rules have one; descriptions do not change this check.

choices.text: It was suppressed with an ignore comment in `main.tf`
choices.why: No comment touched that rule; the only Trivy ignore was `AWS-0132` on the bucket.

choices.text: Trivy reads only one file per resource type
choices.why: It read both files and reported per file.

prompt: Why does Trivy print the `See https://avd.aquasec.com/...` link even in the lab with no network, while Checkov's `Guide:` link is missing?
hint: Where does each link come from?

choices.text: Trivy caches every page of its documentation on first install
choices.why: It prints a link, not a page, and the link is in the check.

choices.text: Checkov hides links in `--compact` mode
choices.why: `checkov-one` ran without `--compact` and still had no `Guide:` line.

choices.text: Trivy's link is part of the check in the binary
choices.why: Right; Checkov's comes from the guidelines download that `--skip-download` turns off.

choices.text: Trivy's links point to a local file
choices.why: The link is an https address; it is simply printed, not fetched.

prompt: tfsec reported twelve results on the shop and none in `ssh.tf`, yet flagged the same rule as `CRITICAL` in `legacy/main.tf`. What explains it?
hint: Compare how the rule is written in each file.

choices.text: Its rules know the inline `ingress` block and not `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule`
choices.why: Yes. A resource type no rule mentions produces silence, which looks like a pass.

choices.text: tfsec skips files other than `main.tf`
choices.why: It reads every `.tf` file; it just had no rule for that resource type.

choices.text: A rule in a file of its own is reviewed, so tfsec trusts it
choices.why: Scanners know nothing about review; they match text against rules.

choices.text: The banner suppresses findings
choices.why: The banner goes to the error stream and changes no result.

prompt: A team keeps tfsec in its pipeline and fears it is missing new resource types. Which practice from the lesson would show that in the build, rather than in an incident?
hint: The lesson used one deliberately bad file.

choices.text: Run tfsec twice and compare the two counts
choices.why: Two runs of the same rules on the same code agree; that finds nothing.

choices.text: Scan a known-bad example in the pipeline and fail if its finding disappears
choices.why: Right. Silence on a file that must fail is the symptom, and the build sees it.

choices.text: Add `--minimum-severity CRITICAL`
choices.why: That shows less, not what the rules cannot see.

choices.text: Suppress every result tfsec gives
choices.why: That removes the findings it does have and says nothing about the missing ones.

prompt: Where does a `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_144:reason` comment go, and what happens to the reason?
hint: Look at the diff Ana wrote.

choices.text: Inside the resource block; it is printed in the report
choices.why: Yes, as `Suppress comment:` under `SKIPPED`.

choices.text: On the line above the block; Checkov discards it
choices.why: That position is Trivy's, and Checkov keeps the reason.

choices.text: In `.checkov.baseline`; it is checked against a ticket number
choices.why: The baseline is a list of check ids per resource; nothing checks tickets.

choices.text: On the command line; it appears in the exit code
choices.why: A command-line skip has no reason, and exit codes carry numbers.

prompt: Trivy reported 11 findings in `main.tf`. Ana adds `#trivy:ignore:AWS-0132:exp:2027-03-31` above the bucket and runs it on 2026-10-02. How many findings does Trivy report in `main.tf` now?
hint: The expiry is in the future.

prompt: Match each finding on the shop with what the lesson did about it.
hint: A suppression is for two of the three kinds of finding.

pairs.right: change the value, not suppress it

pairs.left: `CKV2_AWS_5`: group attached to nothing in this configuration
pairs.right: a false positive, skipped with a reason

pairs.left: `CKV_AWS_144`: no copy in a second region
pairs.right: a cost decision, skipped with a reason

right_distractors: skipped for every resource on the command line

prompt: What happens to a `#trivy:ignore:AWS-0132:exp:...` comment once its date has passed?
hint: Ana moved the date into the past to find out.

choices.text: Trivy deletes the comment from the file
choices.why: Trivy never edits your files; the comment stays and stops working.

choices.text: The finding comes back
choices.why: Yes: `AWS-0132` reappeared and the count went from 10 to 11.

choices.text: Trivy reports the expired comment as a syntax error and stops the scan
choices.why: The scan ran normally and simply included the finding.

choices.text: The finding turns into `LOW`
choices.why: It came back as `HIGH`, its own severity.

prompt: After `cidr_ipv4` became `var.admin_cidr` with no default, Checkov passed `CKV_AWS_24` on the SSH rule. What does that `PASSED` mean?
hint: Could it see the value?

choices.text: That a variable is always safer than a literal
choices.why: The value turned out to be `0.0.0.0/0`; a variable only moved it.

choices.text: Nothing wrong in what it could read
choices.why: Right. With no value there was nothing to fail on, and that reads as a pass.

choices.text: That Checkov read `maintenance.tfvars` automatically
choices.why: It only failed when given `--var-file maintenance.tfvars`.

choices.text: That the rule is restricted to the office range
choices.why: At that point the file said `0.0.0.0/0`; the office range came later.

prompt: Put the steps of a plan scan in order, as Ana ran them.
hint: The scanner reads JSON, not the binary plan.
items: fix the value, then plan and scan again
trap: Checkov cannot read the binary `tfplan` directly; it needs the JSON.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to treat `tfplan.json` like the state file?
hint: Lesson 12 is about the same risk.

choices.text: It is locked during apply
choices.why: Locking is about the state backend, not about this file.

choices.text: Terraform reads it on the next plan
choices.why: Terraform does not read it; it is an export for tools like Checkov.

choices.text: It holds every value in clear, sensitive ones included
choices.why: Yes; keep it out of pull requests and long-lived artefacts.

choices.text: Checkov rewrites it with the findings
choices.why: Checkov only reads it.

prompt: What does `--repo-root-for-plan-enrichment .` add to Checkov's plan scan?
hint: Compare the `File:` lines with and without it.

choices.text: It maps a finding back to the source file and lines
choices.why: Right: `ssh.tf:6-13` with the code, instead of `/tfplan.json:0-0`.

choices.text: It makes Checkov run the plan itself
choices.why: Ana ran `terraform plan` herself; Checkov never calls Terraform.

choices.text: It loads the tfvars files in the root
choices.why: The values were already in the plan.

choices.text: It turns on severities offline
choices.why: Severities still need the download.

prompt: Ana's offline Checkov gate is `--hard-fail-on HIGH`. The scan has nine failed checks. What exit code does it give, and why?
hint: Where do Checkov's severities come from?

choices.text: 1, because nine checks failed and any failure fails the run
choices.why: With `--hard-fail-on` only matching findings fail the run, and none matched.

choices.text: 0, since offline no finding has a severity
choices.why: Yes. The gate passes everything, silently; gate on check ids instead.

choices.text: 2, a usage error for an unknown severity
choices.why: `HIGH` is a valid value; it just matched nothing.

choices.text: 1, because `CKV_AWS_24` is HIGH
choices.why: Offline nothing is HIGH, and `CKV_AWS_24` passed at that point.

prompt: Trivy rates `AWS-0107` (SSH open to any address) and `AWS-0132` (no customer-managed key on the photo bucket) both `HIGH`. What does the lesson say separates them?
hint: The figure has two axes.

choices.text: Their exposure
choices.why: Right: one answers anybody on the internet; the other is a choice of key for public photos.

choices.text: The scanner that found them, since Trivy and Checkov rate the same rule differently
choices.why: Both are Trivy findings with the same severity.

choices.text: The file each finding sits in, because `ssh.tf` was added later
choices.why: Which file holds a rule says nothing about its risk.

choices.text: Their order in the report, which follows risk
choices.why: The report is ordered by check and file, not by risk.

prompt: Ana creates a Checkov baseline, then adds `backups.tf` with a new bucket. Which findings does the next run with `--baseline` report?
hint: A baseline records what is known.

choices.text: All sixteen, old and new together, with the new ones marked so a reviewer can tell them apart
choices.why: The old nine were left out entirely.

choices.text: Only the seven on the new bucket
choices.why: Yes, and the exit code is 1: new code meets the rules.

choices.text: None, because the bucket repeats an existing one and the baseline already lists those checks
choices.why: The baseline is per resource; `aws_s3_bucket.backups` was not in it.

choices.text: Only checks with a severity, which in an offline run means none of them
choices.why: A baseline does not depend on severities.

prompt: tfsec says the shop's bucket *does not have encryption enabled*; Checkov passes `CKV_AWS_19` on it, and Trivy shows `AWS-0088` only with `--include-deprecated-checks`. Which reading fits?
hint: What did S3 change in January 2023?

choices.text: A bug in Checkov that the others caught
choices.why: Trivy agrees with Checkov by retiring its version of the rule.

choices.text: The bucket is unencrypted only in moto, so the tools disagree about the emulator
choices.why: None of the scanners talks to moto; they read the file.

choices.text: A false positive from an older rule
choices.why: Right. S3 encrypts new objects by default now; the rule describes an older AWS.

choices.text: A real problem: add a `#tfsec:ignore` and move on
choices.why: If it were real, suppressing it would be the wrong move; and it is not real.

prompt: A new AWS resource type arrives and the team writes a database's firewall rules with it. Checkov, Trivy and tfsec all report nothing on those files. What should the team conclude first?
hint: Remember what tfsec did with `ssh.tf`.

choices.text: That the rules are safe, since three independent tools agree
choices.why: Three tools whose rules do not know the type agree by silence, which proves nothing.

choices.text: Nothing yet: test a known-bad example first
choices.why: Yes. Silence on an unknown type looks exactly like a pass until a bad file proves the rules can see it.

choices.text: That the scanners need `--skip-download` removed
choices.why: Only Checkov has that flag, and it governs metadata, not which resources the rules know.

choices.text: That a plan scan is required for every new resource type
choices.why: A plan supplies values; it does not teach a rule a resource type it never mentions.

prompt: A module reads `allowed_cidrs` from a variable whose value is set only by the pipeline's environment as `TF_VAR_allowed_cidrs`. Which check would catch a world-open value there?
hint: No file in the repository holds the value.

choices.text: `checkov -d .` on the repository
choices.why: The variable has no value in the files, so the check passes as it did for `admin_cidr`.

choices.text: `checkov -d . --var-file terraform.tfvars`
choices.why: The value is in the environment, not in that file.

choices.text: `tfsec --minimum-severity HIGH`
choices.why: A filter on output does not reveal a value tfsec never saw.

choices.text: A Checkov scan of the plan's JSON
choices.why: Right. The plan is built in the pipeline's environment, so it holds the value.

prompt: Ana is designing the gate for the shop's pipeline. Which of these would make it weaker without anybody noticing? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for gates that pass when they cannot see.

choices.text: Gating offline Checkov on `--hard-fail-on HIGH`
choices.why: Yes; it exits 0 whatever it finds.

choices.text: Gating Trivy on `CRITICAL` alone
choices.why: Yes; it passed this configuration, public-access gaps and all.

choices.text: Gating Checkov on a list of check ids
choices.why: That gate failed as it should, exit code 1.

choices.text: A command-line `--skip-check` for a rule one resource does not need
choices.why: Yes; it silences the rule for every resource, including the next one.

choices.text: An inline skip with a reason, reviewed in the same diff
choices.why: That is the visible kind of exception the lesson recommends.
